sections.text:
One sweltering summer day, as the scorching rays of the sun were drying the land and crops, there was a very hungry and thirsty fox walking slowly in the forest.

The fox had not tasted food or drink for two days, and he was desperately searching for anything to satisfy his hunger and quench his intense thirst.

While he was walking slowly, he came to a beautiful, fenced vineyard, and from behind the fence he saw a large grape vine with huge, ripe, bright purple grape clusters hanging from it.

The grapes looked fresh, full of delicious juice, and shone in the sun in a mouth-watering way.

The fox stopped and looked at the clusters eagerly, and said to himself: “Oh my God! This is exactly what I need now to quench my thirst and satisfy my hunger!”

But the problem was that the clusters were hanging from a very high branch, out of the reach of his short hands and mouth.

The fox took a few steps back, then took a quick start, jumping as hard as he could into the air and catching one of the clusters in his mouth.

But his jump was not enough, and he missed his target and fell hard on his back!
The fox did not give up, so he got up and dusted himself off, and retreated a longer distance this time. He ran more quickly and jumped very high, but again he missed his target by a few centimeters and fell again to the hard ground.

The fox tried a third, fourth, and fifth time.

He was jumping and jumping until his breath was short, his legs hurt, and he felt extremely tired and doubly exhausted due to hunger and thirst.

The fox sat under the vine, panting heavily, looking at the bunches of grapes with great regret and disappointment.

After all these failed attempts, the fox realized that it was impossible to reach that high grape no matter how hard he tried, and that his physical abilities did not allow him to do so.

So, he got up slowly, dragging his tail in disappointment, and in order to hide his failure and save face, he said in a loud voice, as if he was speaking to himself so that those around him could hear:
“Damn these grapes! Anyone who looks at them thinks they are delicious, but I am absolutely sure that they are very sour and rotten, and are not worth all this effort and fatigue in the first place!”

Then he added, walking away with feigned dignity: “I don’t really like sour grapes, and I will not eat them even if they are presented to me on a golden plate!”

He walked away looking for other food, trying to convince himself of this lie to comfort his wounded pride.

From this famous story came the well-known proverb that we give to any person who belittles the value of something that he was unable to achieve or obtain due to his failure and weakness, so he claims that it is a bad thing to justify his inability, so we say to him with a smile: “He sees the grapes as sour!”
